evaluation.positioning_hook: A timid office clerk with erased powers is forced into a monster-hunting squad, and discovers the only way to save the mission is to stop treating his own abilities like a joke.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is immediately legible and has a clean genre promise: oddball workplace fantasy that turns into a monster fight. The appeal is strongest for genre audiences and streamers looking for a quirky ensemble swing, though the very specific humor and world language keep it from feeling four-quadrant.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands fast: Francis is a low-level logistics worker at a bizarre agency, gets drafted onto a suicide mission, and turns out to be the key weapon. The opening pages establish the job, the team, the wrist meter, and the mission with enough clarity to orient the reader quickly.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Francis has a strong underdog engine, and the team around him is colorful enough to support a feature-sized ensemble. The main limitation is that several supporting players are defined more by comic attitude than by deeper contradiction, so the character draw is lively rather than truly durable.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script commits to a weird, retro-futuristic bureaucracy with comic-sans death boards, anomalous powers, and a very specific tonal mashup. It still sits in familiar monster-team territory, but the office-comedy framing and the absurdist dialogue give it a distinct angle.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script moves efficiently from office disruption to team assembly to London mission, and the fight escalates cleanly once the British zombie appears. The middle stretch is more setup-heavy than the action payoff, but the wrist-meter mystery keeps the engine active.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea of a powerless-seeming office drone whose hidden anomaly can erase a monster is fresh enough to feel ownable. It is not yet operating at the level of a fully inevitable premise, but the combination of bureaucratic deadpan and multicolor power expression gives it a memorable signature.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: Comirum feels like a functioning weird workplace, with its logistics division, death-toll board, field-suit hierarchy, and specialized team roles. The world is story-generating and specific, though the mythology is still mostly implied rather than deeply explained.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is unusually committed: deadpan office banter collides with grotesque monster violence and cartoonish bureaucratic absurdity. The dialogue rhythm, the retro-futurist props, and the self-aware team dynamics create a flavor that is hard to mistake for anything else.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Francis’s opening flash of the empty ruins and the erased glasses suggests a larger mystery around his powers and the world’s rules. Right now that depth is more teased than explored, so the script hints at more than it fully delivers on the page.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The team dynamic is the script’s strongest commercial asset: Francis, Ploy, Hal, Clara, Toast, Jerry, and Doreen all generate immediate friction and banter. Even in a single mission, the relationships already feel like a reusable engine rather than a one-off gag.

lead_characters.name: Francis Booker
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 20s to early 30s, working-class office employee with anomalous powers.
lead_characters.hook: Francis is a frightened, self-deprecating logistics clerk who would rather hide behind spreadsheets than become a field operative, but the script keeps revealing that his passivity is a cover for something far stranger. He’s the kind of lead who can play panic, embarrassment, and sudden power in the same beat, and his arc is built around learning that his ‘nothing’ may actually be the most dangerous thing in the room.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Jesse Eisenberg in The Social Network — fast, brittle, funny, and emotionally defensive — with the added bonus of a late-breaking power reveal that lets the actor pivot from comic cowardice to mythic release.

lead_characters.name: Doreen
lead_characters.hook: Doreen is the hard-edged boss who treats absurdity like routine and keeps the whole operation moving with clipped authority and a dry, almost parental contempt. She’s not warm, but she is legible: the person who knows exactly how broken the machine is and still chooses to run it.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Viola Davis in Fences or Jodie Foster in The Silence of the Lambs real command — a contained authority part that lets an actor weaponize stillness, precision, and moral ambiguity.

lead_characters.name: Hal
lead_characters.hook: Hal is the swaggering bruiser who performs confidence as a social shield, even when the room is clearly laughing at him. He gives the team a big, kinetic presence and a comic macho energy that can flip into real competence when the fight starts.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of part that let Dave Bautista or John Cena show they can be funny without losing physical credibility — a role built for a performer who can sell both the joke and the impact.

lead_characters.name: Clara
lead_characters.hook: Clara is a coked-up, knife-catching chaos agent who turns every scene into a dare and every flirtation into a threat. She’s the most combustible member of the team, and the script uses her as both comic voltage and genuine combat danger.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of feral, scene-stealing part that gave Jennifer Lawrence in Silver Linings Playbook or Margot Robbie in Birds of Prey room to be reckless, funny, and physically fearless at once.

lead_characters.name: Toast
lead_characters.demographics: Non-human robot, adult-coded intelligence, masculine presentation.
lead_characters.hook: Toast is the team’s dry, contemptuous robot tactician, all clipped logic and withering judgment, but the script lets him play as more than a machine punchline. He’s the voice of cold competence in a room full of chaos, which makes every insult land harder.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of Alan Tudyk-style voice performance in a character like K-2SO — deadpan precision, comic disdain, and the chance to make a non-human character feel like the smartest person in the room.

lead_characters.name: Ploy
lead_characters.hook: Ploy is loud, flirtatious, physically forceful, and socially fearless, with a bass-heavy entrance that announces her before she even speaks. She’s the team member who most directly pulls Francis into the mission and into the emotional logic of the story.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of high-energy, swagger-heavy supporting role that lets an actor do what Awkwafina did in The Farewell or what a breakout in an ensemble comedy does — steal scenes through rhythm, confidence, and specificity.

lead_characters.name: Jerry
lead_characters.hook: Jerry is a friendly, hungry, physically distinctive office creature whose casual appetite makes the world feel lived-in and strange. He’s not central to the plot, but he adds texture and a sense that Comirum is full of odd beings with their own routines.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of prosthetic-heavy, personality-forward role that gives an actor or performer the fun of creature work without losing comic humanity — the sort of part that can become a cult favorite if played with commitment.

casting_characteristics: ensemble with several highly stylized supporting roles
multilingual or accent-specific dialogue for Ploy and Clara

technical.vfx_details: Multicolor energy effects, erasure/flashback visuals, glitch effects on the zombie, and a transforming weapon gag; creature enhancement likely needed for the British zombie and the cyborg wolf-man.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical blood, prosthetic wounds, arm loss, head burst/regeneration beats, breakaway glass, weapon transformation props, and impact gags.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: ensemble genre film with a contained mission structure and franchise-adjacent worldbuilding.

budget.note: The contemporary office material is cheap, but the London night exteriors, creature work, energy effects, and prosthetic violence will push this above a simple contained indie if not tightly scoped.

casting.note: Francis needs a lead who can play anxious comedy, latent power, and emotional release, while Clara, Ploy, Hal, and Toast all need sharply differentiated performers to keep the ensemble from flattening.

development.note: The script has a clear engine, but the mythology around SINONs, the wrist meter, and the erased opening image is still more suggestive than fully dramatized, which makes the premise feel slightly ahead of its explanation.

comp_set.title: The Suicide Squad
comp_set.why_it_comps: A ragtag government team of misfits, violent comic-book action, and a tone that treats absurdity as part of the operating system.

comp_set.title: The Boys
comp_set.why_it_comps: The script shares the same appetite for grotesque powers, irreverent banter, and a world where institutional dysfunction is the joke and the threat.

comp_set.title: Free Guy
comp_set.why_it_comps: A low-status protagonist discovers he is secretly the key to a larger system, with comedy built from a character waking up inside a bizarre ruleset.

comp_set.title: Guardians of the Galaxy
comp_set.why_it_comps: The ensemble chemistry, oddball team assembly, and playful genre confidence echo the same crowd-pleasing misfit-team appeal.

audience_target.primary_audience: Genre fans who like irreverent ensemble action-comedy with a weird mythology and a lovable underdog lead.
audience_target.demographics: 18-44, skewing male but with real crossover for viewers who respond to character-driven genre comedy and stylized team dynamics.

budget_tier.note: The office material is inexpensive, but the creature effects, night exterior action, prosthetic violence, and ensemble cast put this in mid-budget feature territory.

types_of_buyers: IP-minded development execs looking for franchise-adjacent worldbuilding
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane of irreverent, character-forward genre films that can sell on concept, ensemble chemistry, and a distinctive world. The script’s mix of office satire, monster violence, and retro-futurist design makes it attractive to buyers who want something weird but still legible.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature: the page establishes a fun team and a larger agency world, but no side character or world element is yet deep enough to justify a clear sequel or spinoff vector.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The opening image is a strong mystery engine.
strengths.what_it_means: The ruined college flash and the erased glasses create an immediate question that can sell curiosity before the comedy even lands. That kind of visual hook is useful for trailers, pitch decks, and any buyer looking for a genre promise with a mythic undertow.
strengths.evidence: Francis wakes in the college ruins, sees the abandoned belongings and cracked glasses, and bleeds from the nose before cutting back to the office.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Francis is a clean underdog lead.
strengths.what_it_means: A timid office worker who turns out to be the key weapon is a commercially legible protagonist with built-in audience identification. That gives casting and marketing a simple emotional spine: the guy nobody takes seriously becomes the one who saves the mission.
strengths.evidence: Francis insists he is not a field guy, repeatedly denies his usefulness, then finally triggers the multicolor beam that destroys the zombie.

strengths.what_it_means: The team banter creates reusable value beyond the first mission, which is a major asset for buyers who want a movie that feels like a group rather than a single gimmick. Ensemble chemistry also broadens the casting conversation because the movie can be sold through interplay, not just plot.
strengths.evidence: Hal’s macho bluster, Clara’s chaos, Toast’s contempt, Ploy’s teasing, and Doreen’s deadpan authority all land in the first half of the script.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The tone is specific and marketable.
strengths.what_it_means: The script’s deadpan bureaucracy plus absurd monster violence gives it a distinct flavor that can stand out in a crowded genre field. Buyers chasing elevated-but-fun genre material will recognize the lane immediately.
strengths.evidence: Comic-sans death board, retro-futuristic wrist device, and a British zombie who speaks in grotesque tea-time clichés.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The world feels operational, not decorative.
strengths.what_it_means: Comirum has enough internal structure to support story momentum without needing a giant exposition dump. That makes the project easier to package as a repeatable universe rather than a one-joke premise.
strengths.evidence: Logistics division, field suits, outburst meter, article-based termination language, and mission briefing hierarchy.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, sellable genre package: a misfit-team action-comedy with a memorable lead, a weird bureaucratic world, and enough creature/action business to justify a mid-budget swing. The ensemble chemistry and opening mystery give it both trailer value and development upside, which is exactly the combination buyers want in streaming-friendly elevated genre.

items.area: The mythology is still mostly a tease.
items.detail: The opening ruins image, the wrist meter, and the SINON label all imply a larger system, but the script keeps that system at arm’s length. That makes the premise easy to enjoy in the moment, but it also means the buyer is mostly buying tone and ensemble rather than a fully articulated world.

items.area: Francis’s power rules are intentionally fuzzy.
items.detail: The script leans on the idea that he can 'do anything' once the meter hits the right point, but the trigger logic is still opaque by design. That fuzziness is part of the joke, but it also narrows the clarity of the action engine until the rules are more legible.

items.area: The supporting team is vivid before it is deep.
items.detail: Hal, Clara, Toast, and Ploy all pop immediately, but most of their characterization is built from voice, attitude, and one-note comic behavior in the mission sequence. That is enough for a first impression, but a producer would still see room for deeper contradiction if the goal is to make the ensemble feel premium rather than merely fun.

items.area: The London fight carries the budget.
items.detail: The night exterior, rooftop coverage, creature regeneration, prosthetic damage, and energy-beam climax are the expensive stretch of the script. If this is greenlit, those pages will be the first place a line producer starts pressure-testing scope.

issues.headline: The main friction is clarity versus vibe: the script has a strong tone and a fun team, but the larger SINON mythology and Francis’s power logic are still more suggestive than fully owned. On the production side, the London creature fight is the budget conversation every buyer will have to have before saying yes.
